summary: The narrator, badly injured and tortured, speaks with Professor Martinez while captors (the Lancer and his men) watch. She reflects that she can choose to be someone who trusts, believing in certain people such as Arthur, Checker and herself rather than faith in general. The narrator urges Martinez to act bothered and to convince the captors they are getting to her so they keep the torture on the narrator rather than others. When the Lancer demands information, Martinez pleads for him to stop, and he responds by striking the narrator's cheek. The excerpt ends with the narrator's body seizing in pain.
one_line: Tortured narrator urges Professor Martinez to play along with the Lancer's captors while clinging to faith in certain people.
key_facts: The narrator is badly injured and in pain, questioning whether she is hallucinating or only thinking words during the torture.
The narrator says, "Faith," when asked how she knows the rescuers will come, and reflects she could choose to be someone who trusted.
Martinez says, "I don't believe in faith," calling it "the antithesis of evidence-based science."
The narrator decides she only needs to believe in certain people: Arthur, Checker, and Myself most of all.
The narrator tells Martinez, "Act like this bothers you," so the captors keep drawing it out on her and not anyone else.
The narrator suggests Martinez tell the captors she will give them something if they stop, beg them, then take it back.
The Lancer leans on his walking stick, pinning Martinez with an intense stare "like she was a butterfly on a card."
Martinez makes eye contact with the narrator for the first time, and her eyes go large.
Martinez pleads with the Lancer, "Please stop this," and he replies, "Tell me what I want to know, and we'll stop."
The Lancer nods to his men, and he smacks the narrator's cheek, which she cannot feel.
The narrator's whole body is seizing, described as "a thousand million tiny internal catastrophes."
